It planned to mass 2,500 people with 31,000 more on standby, and actually gathered about 11,000. On the evening of October 9, Ma Tianshui phoned to say “they are in good health,” and Xu Jingxian and Wang Xiuzhen at once called off most of the gathering. At a meeting on Kangping Road on the night of the 12th, Zhu Yongjia of the writing group urged seizing the radio station, the newspapers and the airport, and Chen Ada said they could sink ships to block the river and park trucks on the runways. Shi Shangying of the Militia Command would not move troops. After the meeting he ordered every district by telegram not to act without authorization. He later said his idea was simply to stall. On the 13th Ma Tianshui, Xu Jingxian and Wang Xiuzhen came back to Shanghai to relay instructions, and the matter was dropped. A few days later Shanghai residents held spontaneous parades to celebrate.

History Huang Jinhai said that on the afternoon of October 13 he told the factory Party secretary to “press the bullets into the militia's magazines, but keep the guns and ammunition stored separately.” See “Ten Years Not a Dream” (《十年非梦》), ch. 11.
1896:

You got out of the car south of the monument. Nobody recognized you. In your old Mao suit you looked like any of the workers in the square.

You walked among the wreaths. A young man on the steps was copying poems, writing fast. You leaned in to look. He was copying one that attacked Jiang Qing. A few pages on was one that attacked you. He looked up at you and said, comrade, are you copying too?

You stood in the square all afternoon. After dark you rode back to Zhongnanhai. The Politburo met again to decide what to call the square.
1897: “I was in the square this afternoon. There are no counterrevolutionaries there. They are ordinary people.”
1898: You did not say you had been to the square. When it came to the vote, you did not raise your hand.
1899: Fiction The entrance to the dream of “standing with the people at Tiananmen” (A8). In history Wang Hongwen never went to the square.
1903:

The duty office made call after call. Some military regions said understood. Some said they had to ask for instructions. The Beijing Military Region did not answer.

Eight o'clock passed. Huairen Hall waited for you and did not get you, and did not get Zhang Chunqiao either. What came was a call from Jiang Qing asking Hua Guofeng why he was calling a meeting. Hua Guofeng told her on the phone that the meeting was postponed.

Nobody slept that night. Ye Jianying left Zhongnanhai for the Western Hills. Wang Dongxing's guard units held the gates of Zhongnanhai, and your duty office was inside Zhongnanhai. Each side was waiting for the other to move first.

Near dawn Zhang Chunqiao came to see you. He said there was only one way now. Call a Central Committee plenum and let the more than two hundred Central Committee members vote. The Chairman had said while he was alive that we must unite with the more than two hundred Central Committee members.
1905: “Before the plenum, take Ye Jianying and Wang Dongxing into custody.”
1906: Fiction The entrance to the dream of “the Gang of Four wins” (C1). In history Wang Hongwen did not see through the arrangement at Huairen Hall. On May 3, 1975, Mao Zedong said, “Why not unite with the more than two hundred Central Committee members,” quoted in Huang Jinhai, ch. 11, from “A Brief History of the Cultural Revolution” (《“文化大革命”简史》).
1907: He went to Tiananmen Square? I don't believe it. If he really did, that was his own business and had nothing to do with the Workers' General Headquarters.
1908: Wang Hongwen wavered during April Fifth. We heard about that in Shanghai too.
1909: The point of this dream is to look at April 1976 and October 1976 together. Both times the fate of the square was decided inside Zhongnanhai. Only the people deciding had changed.
1910: If we had been the ones who won that year, I can't say what would have happened. All I know is that in the year we lost, Shanghai sentenced several hundred people.
1911: If that day in October had gone the other way, I would probably have been a Party secretary in Shanghai for many years. I thought about that many times in prison.
1912: A “Gang of Four” victory would not mean the goals of the Cultural Revolution came true. Its most likely result was a more rigid regime and a delayed collapse that might have been more violent.
1913: He phoned from Beijing and told Shanghai to act, and that is how he ruined the Shanghai militia. People died that week, and those of us who never fired a shot got heavy sentences too.
1914: Early on October 9, Chen Ada phoned and told me to go back to the mill and get tea ready. I thought he had come back to Shanghai. Only when I got there did I learn he had been arrested. We set up a few posts in Shanghai and drafted 21 slogans. On the 13th Ma Tianshui came back and told us not to move, and we all stood down. Not one militiaman went into the streets. Later they called it an armed rebellion. ⟦0⟧
1915: He did tell the militia to step things up in '75. I don't deny that.
1916: He made that call and Wang Xiuzhen took it. Everything after started with that call.
1917: After October 6, it was mostly a few of us holding things together in Shanghai. On the 13th, back from Beijing, I relayed the news in the small auditorium of the Jinjiang Hotel. The people below could not accept it. Some cried. We could not accept it ourselves. ⟦0⟧
1918: Setting up the duty office in Zhongnanhai handed the other side a pretext.
1919: In history, the “Shanghai armed rebellion” was closer to a charge than an event. It never really happened. This dream makes it happen only to show who would bear the cost if it had.
1920: The “smashing of the Gang of Four” in October 1976 was an arrest carried out in the name of the Central Committee. Shanghai prepared to resist from October 8 to 13 and called it off after the 13th. The official account called it “smashing the plot for an armed rebellion in Shanghai.” Those involved were later sentenced, though Huang Jinhai and others held that the charge lacked a factual basis. Wang Hongwen himself had no chance to do anything. He was pinned down at the door of Huairen Hall.
1921: He had just married. On October 5 he came back to Beijing and went to tell Cui Gendi about the divorce for you.
1922: She said she would agree if she could have the children. You were arrested before the paperwork was done. Later she said, he is still young, and he came from a hard life. I will wait for him.
1923: He was taken away from the security section of No. 31 Mill, on charges heavier than in history.
1924: Early on October 9 he was called back to the mill to get tea ready, and he thought you had come back to Shanghai. He was later sentenced to fifteen years.
1925: In Shanghai he argued for fighting, saying even if they could not hold out a week, three days would do. He was later sentenced to fourteen years.
1926: He was held in the warehouse for three months. When he was rehabilitated in 1978, he got his notebook of copied poems back.
1927: He was held in the warehouse for half a year. When he was rehabilitated in 1978, the notebook of copied poems was never found.
1928: He was arrested at Huairen Hall the same evening as you. Afterward, in court, he never said a word.
1929:
In history, in 1975 Wang Hongwen inspected militia weapons in Shanghai and called for stepped-up training. In February 1976 Hua Guofeng took charge of the Central Committee's work. In April the April Fifth Movement was declared a counterrevolutionary incident, and Wang Hongwen told Shanghai to step up combat readiness. In July came the Tangshan earthquake. On September 9 Mao Zedong died, and on the 11th Wang Hongwen set up a separate duty office in Zhongnanhai. On October 5 he asked Liao Zukang to tell Cui Gendi he wanted a divorce. On the evening of the 6th he was arrested at Huairen Hall, along with Zhang Chunqiao, Jiang Qing and Yao Wenyuan. From October 8 to 13 Shanghai prepared to resist, setting up liaison posts, drafting slogans and putting the militia on alert. All of it was called off on the 13th, after Ma Tianshui and the others came back from Beijing to relay instructions. In November a central work group announced that “a counterrevolutionary armed rebellion has been smashed.”

From Anting to Huairen Hall, ten years less one month.
1933: You wake up. This time, the line in the indictment came true.
1934: You wake up. The corridor light is on. This time, you dreamed of the very day you came here.
1939: Special Court of the Supreme People's Court
1940: From November 20, 1980 to January 25, 1981, it tried the ten principal defendants of the “Lin Biao and Jiang Qing counterrevolutionary cliques.” Wang Hongwen faced five charges, namely organizing and leading a counterrevolutionary clique, plotting to subvert the government, inciting armed rebellion, counterrevolutionary injury, and false accusation. The specifics included Kangping Road, Shanghai Diesel Liansi, compiling “A Small Collection of Chen Yi's Reactionary Remarks,” and building a “second armed force” in Shanghai. The Anting Incident was not among them. Wang Hongwen pleaded guilty to everything, did not hire a defense lawyer, and was sentenced to life imprisonment. Zhang Chunqiao said nothing throughout. Jiang Qing argued back in court.
1943: From December 1976 the Central Committee issued, in installments, the “Evidence of the Crimes of the Wang Hongwen, Zhang Chunqiao, Jiang Qing, Yao Wenyuan Anti-Party Clique,” Nos. 1, 2 and 3, sent to grassroots organizations nationwide for study. The section on Wang Hongwen listed color TVs, cameras, cigars, watches and other items he had “forcibly demanded” from the Shanghai Light Industry Bureau, as well as the costs of food, water, electricity and cars at his Shanghai residence. These materials were denunciations made within the investigation campaign and used for nationwide criticism. They were never independently verified and are not court evidence.
1946: Former head of the General Logistics Department and a member of the Lin Biao clique, held in Qincheng around the same time as Wang Hongwen. His memoir says that after his arrest Wang Hongwen was subjected to restraints, sleep deprivation and forced injections, and that during exercise time he “fell straight to the ground like a door plank.” This is secondhand, comes from another defendant, and cannot be verified. Use it with special care.
1948: Wang Hongwen's wife, a worker at No. 17 State Cotton Mill, whose parents were both workers. In October 1976 Wang Hongwen asked Liao Zukang to tell her he wanted a divorce. She said she would agree if she could have the children. The paperwork was not finished before Wang Hongwen was arrested. Later the organization called her in for a talk, and she said, “Wang Hongwen committed crimes. However you sentence him is not my business, but I won't divorce him. He is still young, and he came from a hard life. I will wait for him.” After that, every year on their wedding anniversary, October 1, she took the children to visit him at Qincheng. She died on April 14, 2026.
1951: A hospital under the Ministry of Public Security. In 1985 a medical exam found that Wang Hongwen had serious liver disease, and he was moved here, the same hospital where Zhang Chunqiao was. He died of liver cancer on August 3, 1992, at 56. Xinhua issued a dispatch the next day, and on August 5 the People's Daily ran it in the lower right corner of page two.
1953: A physics student at East China Normal University. After October 1976 he wrote letters criticizing Shanghai for continuing to criticize Deng and arguing that Deng Xiaoping should return to work. He was sentenced to death for active counterrevolution and shot. Later his family and the university hired lawyers and won the case, and the Liberation Daily reported it on the front page. See Huang Jinhai, “Ten Years Not a Dream” (《十年非梦》), ch. 12 (paraphrased). This shows that punishment for speech did not stop right away after October 1976.
1957:
They held you in a basement. The room was small, with a bed and a table, and the light was always on. There was a small window in the door, and every so often someone outside looked in.

For the first few months it was talks. Later it was writing. They gave you a stack of paper and told you to write a confession, starting from 1966. You wrote about Anting, Kangping Road, Shanghai Diesel, Changsha. When you finished one, they took it away, brought it back a few days later, said it was not enough, write it again.

You could not sleep well. Later you told other prisoners that something in the room went off at set times. It was not loud, but it bored into you, and you could fall asleep while drinking water. You said they gave you injections, and after them you could not sleep at all. These words came out through another prisoner's memoir. No one can confirm them.

In December the Central Committee issued a set of materials that included your “evidence of crimes.” Your keeper laid them on the table, opened them, and pointed. They listed how many color TVs, cameras, cigars and watches you took from the Shanghai Light Industry Bureau, and how much water, electricity and coal your residence in Shanghai used in three and a half months. The last line said, Wang Hongwen the bloodsucker.
1958: On the first night you thought of that Book of the Later Han. You had told Zhu Yongjia the Chairman meant you should not be another Liu Penzi. You never did become Liu Penzi. After Liu Penzi surrendered, Liu Xiu gave him a plot of land.
1959: On the first night you thought of the question Zhu Yongjia could not answer. What was planted on Liu Penzi's land. You still do not know.
